questions.question: What's the fastest thing in the universe?
questions.reveal: In a vacuum, light covers nearly 300,000 kilometres every second.

questions.question: Which type of heat transfer can travel through the vacuum of space?
questions.reveal: That's how the Sun's heat reaches us across about 150 million kilometres of empty space.

questions.question: What is the unit of force?
questions.reveal: Named after Isaac Newton, who famously wondered why apples fall.

questions.question: Is sound a transverse wave or a longitudinal wave?
questions.reveal: Air particles squash together and spread apart in the same direction the sound travels.

questions.question: Why can't sound travel through space?
questions.reveal: Sound needs a medium like air, water or rock. In space, no one can hear you scream.

questions.question: Heat moving up a metal spoon sitting in hot soup is an example of which type of heat transfer?
questions.reveal: Vibrating particles pass the energy along to their neighbours, all the way up the handle.

questions.question: What is the unit of energy?
questions.reveal: Named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule.

questions.question: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.reveal: Violet is at the other end of the rainbow, with the shortest wavelength.

questions.question: Newton's second law says force equals mass times what?
questions.reveal: Push twice as hard on the same mass and it accelerates twice as fast.

questions.question: Why do you see lightning before you hear the thunder?
questions.reveal: Count the seconds between flash and boom, divide by three, and that's roughly how many kilometres away it is.

questions.question: What's the name for light bending as it passes from air into water?
questions.reveal: That's why a straw looks bent in a glass of water.

questions.question: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum gives you sunburn?
questions.reveal: UV can burn you even on a cloudy day, so slip, slop, slap!

questions.question: Hot air rising and cooler air sinking to form a current is called what?
questions.reveal: It's why the top floor of a house is often the warmest.

questions.question: On the Moon, would your mass or your weight be smaller?
questions.reveal: Your mass stays the same, but the Moon's gravity is only about one sixth of Earth's.

questions.question: What is the unit used to measure frequency?
questions.reveal: One hertz means one complete wave every second.

questions.question: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. What is this law called?
questions.reveal: The total energy in a closed system always stays the same.

questions.question: What type of energy does any moving object have?
questions.reveal: The word comes from the Greek for 'to move'.

questions.question: Which electromagnetic waves are used to see broken bones in hospital?
questions.reveal: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered them in 1895 and won the first ever Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.question: What do we call sound that's too high-pitched for humans to hear?
questions.reveal: That's above about 20,000 hertz. Bats use it to find food in the dark.

questions.question: What is the force that slows down a sliding object?
questions.reveal: Without it, you couldn't even walk without slipping over.

questions.question: Does sound travel faster through air or through steel?
questions.reveal: Sound moves more than ten times faster through steel than through air.

questions.question: What do we call the distance from one wave crest to the next?
questions.reveal: Long wavelengths sound low; short wavelengths sound high.

questions.question: Which type of electromagnetic wave do most TV remotes use?
questions.reveal: Point a remote at your phone camera and press a button: you may see it flash.

questions.question: 'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.' Which of Newton's laws is this?
questions.reveal: Rockets push gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.

questions.question: What does a sound wave's frequency decide: its pitch or its loudness?
questions.reveal: Higher frequency means a higher pitch. The amplitude decides how loud it is.

questions.question: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.reveal: The sunlight hitting you right now left the Sun around eight minutes ago.

questions.question: What kind of energy is stored in a stretched rubber band?
questions.reveal: Let it go and that stored energy turns into kinetic energy.

questions.question: Speed in a particular direction is called what?
questions.reveal: Fifty kilometres per hour is a speed. Fifty kilometres per hour heading north is a velocity.

questions.question: Which electromagnetic waves have the highest energy?
questions.reveal: They come from radioactive decay and some of the most violent explosions in the universe.

questions.question: White light splits into a rainbow when it passes through which triangular glass object?
questions.reveal: Isaac Newton used prisms to show that white light is a mix of all the colours.

questions.question: What force pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth?
questions.reveal: It's also what keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth.

questions.question: Roughly how fast does sound travel through air?
questions.reveal: That's at 20 degrees Celsius. Sound travels a little faster in warmer air.

questions.question: What is the unit of electric current?
questions.reveal: Short for ampere, after the French physicist André-Marie Ampère.

questions.question: Without air resistance, which hits the ground first: a hammer or a feather dropped at the same time?
questions.reveal: Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott tested it on the Moon in 1971, and they landed together.

questions.question: What is the height of a wave from its rest position to its crest called?
questions.reveal: The bigger the amplitude of a sound wave, the louder it sounds.

questions.question: Which metal is most often used for the wires in household electrical cables?
questions.reveal: It's an excellent conductor, and far cheaper than silver, the best conductor of all.

questions.question: In a transverse wave, which way do the particles move compared with the direction the wave travels?
questions.reveal: Like a Mexican wave: people move up and down while the wave travels around the stadium.

questions.question: Which electromagnetic waves have the longest wavelengths?
questions.reveal: Some radio waves are kilometres long.

questions.question: What do we call materials like rubber and plastic that stop electricity flowing easily?
questions.reveal: That's why electrical wires are wrapped in plastic.

questions.question: What is the upward force from a liquid that keeps a boat afloat called?
questions.reveal: It's also called upthrust.

questions.question: Which scientist won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry for her work on radioactivity?
questions.reveal: She's still the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

questions.question: Roughly how much speed does a falling object gain each second on Earth, ignoring air resistance?
questions.reveal: That's the acceleration due to gravity: about 9.8 metres per second squared.

questions.question: The time it takes for half of a radioactive substance to decay is called what?
questions.reveal: Carbon-14's half-life is about 5,700 years, which is how we date ancient bones.

questions.question: What's the name for a sound wave bouncing back off a cliff or a wall?
questions.reveal: Bats and dolphins use echoes to work out where things are.

questions.question: Do radio waves, visible light and X-rays all travel at the same speed in a vacuum?
questions.reveal: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the speed of light in a vacuum.

questions.question: When a bus brakes suddenly, why do the passengers lurch forward?
questions.reveal: Newton's first law: your body keeps moving until a force stops it.

questions.question: In a petrol car engine, most of the fuel's energy is lost as which form of energy?
questions.reveal: Only a small share of the fuel's energy actually moves the car.

questions.question: What is the name for waves spreading out as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle?
questions.reveal: That's why you can hear someone talking around a corner, even when you can't see them.

questions.question: What do we call the part of a sound wave where the air particles are squashed closest together?
questions.reveal: The spread-out parts in between are called rarefactions.

questions.question: In Einstein's famous equation, E equals m c squared, what does the c stand for?
questions.reveal: It's such a huge number that a tiny bit of mass holds an enormous amount of energy.
